Kofi winced at the sight of his own knees drifting inward, yet he was also grateful, because a mirror cannot always show what a camera can. After that he corrected it at once, and the next video looked noticeably better.

Kofi finished his tenth squat, slowly and carefully, and stood there with his thighs trembling pleasantly and his face split by a grin. Ana gave him a thumbs up and told him that this humble movement was the base of much of what they would do together. He had expected to hate his first lesson, and he found that he was already planning the second.

Ana stood sideways to the mirror and pushed her hips back, as if she were closing a car door with her bottom. That, she said, is the hinge, and it means folding forward from the hips instead of bending from the waist like a hairpin. It sounded easy, and it turned out to be more difficult than it sounded.

To help him feel it, Ana laid a long wooden stick down the length of his spine and asked him to bend forward without letting it move. If the stick touched the back of his head, the middle of his back and the base of his spine all the way down, then his back was holding its natural shape. The first time, it wobbled away from him like a leaf in the wind.

Kofi bent forward and curled his back into a perfect cat's arch, and Ana laughed so loudly that Tomas looked up from the desk. A rounded back is the most common mistake among beginners, she told him, and it is the one that causes the most worry later. The cure is to keep the back long and to let the hips do the folding.

When he finally managed a good hinge, Kofi felt a pleasant stretch along the backs of his thighs, and his knees stayed gently bent instead of locking. Ana explained that the large muscles behind the legs and in the bottom are the engine of this movement, and that they are among the strongest in the body. For years Kofi's own muscles, she observed with a grin, had been sitting in an office chair doing nothing at all.

Ana placed a light dumbbell on the floor in front of him and told him to hinge down, take hold of it and stand up again. He kept the weight close to his legs, as though it were a sleeping cat that he did not wish to disturb, and he held his back long and straight. The dumbbell rose smoothly from the floor, and Kofi felt a small, unexpected thrill of success.

The deadlift, Ana explained, is nothing more than a hinge with a weight in your hands, which was good news for someone who had just learned the hinge. She set a barbell loaded with two small plates on rubber blocks so that it began a little above the floor, and she assured him that nobody would ask for heroics. The bar looked friendly enough, but Kofi knew perfectly well that it was still a real bar and deserved respect.

Kofi stood with the bar above the middle of his feet and took hold of it just outside his knees, his grip firm but not desperate. Ana asked him to keep his back flat and his shoulders over the bar, and then she told him to imagine pushing the floor away with his legs. This simple image worked far better than any long explanation of muscles, and his legs seemed to understand it at once.

At the top of the lift Kofi stood tall, with his shoulders back and his chest open, and Ana tapped his lower back to remind him not to lean. The aim was simply to stand up straight, she said, because the hips and knees should finish straightening together and nothing more is needed. Leaning backward adds strain to the lower back and gives no extra benefit, so it is a habit worth avoiding.

Lowering the bar, Ana explained, is as important as lifting it, and it is done in exactly the opposite order. Kofi sent his hips back first, let the bar slide down past his knees under control and put it gently on the rubber blocks without any crash. He was beginning to understand that strength, in the end, was mostly a quiet and stubborn form of patience.

At home that evening, Kofi bent to pick up his basket of laundry, and without thinking he sent his hips back and kept his back long. The basket rose with no groan and no effort, and he stood in the hallway holding it, absurdly proud of himself. For years he had lifted things badly, and now, at last, he understood why it had always felt like a battle.

Pushing, Ana told him, simply means pressing something away from your body, and it can be learned without any equipment at all. She led Kofi to a bare wall, asked him to lean against it with his arms straight and then to push himself away, and he did it feeling slightly foolish. It was, nonetheless, the first honest push of his whole training, and it felt oddly satisfying.

For the next exercise Kofi placed his hands on a sturdy bench and lowered his chest toward it, with his body in one straight line from head to heels. This press-up works the chest, the shoulders and the backs of the arms, Ana said, and it is much gentler than the same movement on the floor. Even so, his arms were trembling pleasantly by the eighth repetition, and he had to rest.

The beauty of a press-up, Ana explained, is that it can be made easier or harder simply by changing the angle of the body. A higher surface makes it easier and a lower one makes it harder, so everybody can find a version that challenges them without breaking their form. Kofi chose the middle bench and promised himself that he would visit the lower ones in time.

Standing tall with a light dumbbell in each hand, Kofi pressed the weights slowly above his head until his arms were straight. Ana reminded him to keep his ribs down and his bottom gently tucked, because arching the back puts the effort in the wrong place and invites discomfort. A small, steady press with good form, she said, is worth a dozen showy ones done badly.

The shoulder, Ana told him, is one of the most flexible joints in the body, which also makes it one of the easiest to irritate. Before pressing, Kofi rolled both shoulders in slow circles, and he promised to stop at once if he felt a sharp pinch rather than the dull effort of working muscles. Ordinary effort is welcome, she said, but a sharp warning should always be respected.

To pull, Ana said, means to draw a weight towards your body, and it is the natural partner of the push. Kofi sat at a cable machine, took hold of the handle and brought it slowly to his chest, squeezing his shoulder blades together at the end of each repetition. He could feel muscles in the middle of his back that he had never known he possessed.

At the weights bench, Kofi put one hand and one knee on the pad and lifted a dumbbell with his free arm, as if he were starting a small lawnmower. His elbow travelled back towards his hip, and Ana explained that the movement should be felt in the back rather than in the arm. After five repetitions he swapped sides and was surprised that the left one was weaker.

At the pulldown machine, Kofi sat on a padded seat, held a long bar above his head and drew it slowly down to his chest. The machine lets a beginner choose the weight precisely, Ana said, so it is a friendly way to train the muscles used for pull-ups long before one can do a real one. Kofi, who could not do a pull-up and had no intention of trying, found this reassuring.

On the whiteboard Ana drew two office workers, one with a rounded back and drooping shoulders, the other sitting tall and relaxed. We spend our days pushing and reaching forward, she explained, so pulling exercises help to balance the body and strengthen the muscles that hold us upright. The picture of the first worker looked uncomfortably like Kofi at his own desk on any normal day.

The next morning at the office, Kofi noticed something odd: he was sitting a little taller, and his shoulders were no longer creeping up around his ears. For the first time in years he could feel the muscles of his back, a quiet and satisfied ache in just the right place. He did not mention it to anyone, but he smiled at his screen all morning.

Ana handed Kofi a heavy dumbbell for each hand and told him, with the air of a person giving directions, to walk across the room. The carry means holding weights while you move, she said, and its simplest form is called the farmer's walk, after the way a farmer might carry heavy loads. It looked like the easiest exercise of all, which is exactly why it is so deceptive.

Kofi set off across the gym floor at the pace of a man carrying two full cups of tea, standing tall with his shoulders back and the weights hanging beside him. Ana walked alongside, watching for any lean or sway, and reminded him to keep his steps small and steady and his eyes forward. By the time he reached the far wall he was breathing hard and grinning.

Halfway across the room Kofi felt his fingers begin to burn, and his knuckles turned the colour of candle wax as he gripped the handles. A carry tests the grip more than almost any other exercise, Ana said, and a stronger grip is quietly useful in a hundred everyday places. Jars, door handles, shopping bags and heavy suitcases all depend on it, and so does a firm handshake.

Ana then gave him a single kettlebell and asked him to carry it in his right hand while keeping the rest of his body upright. The weight tried to pull him sideways, and the muscles in the middle of his body, which he had hardly noticed before, worked hard to stop it. It felt as if his waist had suddenly become a pair of invisible hands, holding him upright against the pull.

Ana pointed to a diagram of the trunk on the wall and explained that the core is the group of muscles around the middle of the body, at the front, the sides and the back. Their main job is to keep the body steady while the arms and legs move, and they do far more than the stomach muscles seen in advertisements. Kofi studied the drawing for a long moment, with a new and slightly surprised respect for his own middle.

Watching Kofi slouch over his phone between sets, Ana asked him whether he thought there was a perfect posture. She told him that most physiotherapists would say no, because the body is made to move, and that changing position often matters just as much as standing tall. Strength, however, makes it easier to hold whichever position he chooses, and to enjoy the change when it comes.

After a week of lessons Kofi did something he would never have attempted before: he carried all his shopping from the car to his front door in a single trip, with one bag in each hand. Carrying evenly, as Ana had shown him, felt far steadier than hauling one bag and leaning like a tilted tower. He did not even need to put the bags down once on the way to the door.

The stairs to his flat were a different matter, because carrying a load uphill makes any weight feel heavier and any breath shorter. Kofi began slowly, took the bags one flight at a time and paused once on the landing, which Ana later told him was perfectly sensible. Pride, she said with a laugh, is a poor reason to rush a staircase, and a very good reason to take it carefully.

When a carry is finished, Ana told him, the weights should be put down with the same care with which they were picked up. Kofi bent his knees and hinged at the hips to lower the dumbbells to the floor, and he took care to keep his feet well clear, because a dropped weight can easily injure a toe. It was another small habit, and he was glad that he had learned it early, before it could become a bad one.

At the end of the lesson Kofi walked up to the whiteboard and ticked five boxes in a neat row: squat, hinge, push, pull and carry. Ana told him that, with these five movements, he now had the foundation for almost every other exercise in the gym, and that everything else was a variation on a theme. He looked at the ticks for a long moment, as proud as if he had won a prize.

Kofi arrived straight from a cold street, still wearing his coat and carrying his bag, and made straight for the barbell with the eagerness of a new convert. Ana caught his sleeve and gently turned him around, explaining that the first thing he needed to lift today was his own heart rate. A body that begins work cold, she said, is a body that has not yet agreed to cooperate.

A warm-up, Ana told him, raises the heart rate, warms the muscles and prepares the joints, and it is widely recommended for helping the body to move smoothly and perform well. Whether it actually prevents injuries is less certain, since the research is mixed, but nobody doubts that it makes the first set feel better. It also offers the mind a few minutes in which to switch from the office to the gym.

For the beginning, Ana suggested five to ten minutes of light movement, such as cycling, brisk walking or a gentle session on the rowing machine. Kofi chose the stationary bike and pedalled at an easy pace, watching the clock and waiting for the gentle warmth that creeps into the skin when the blood begins to move. After seven minutes he was breathing a little faster and felt, for the first time that day, genuinely awake.

Next came a minute of mobility, as Ana called it: Kofi swung each leg forwards and backwards, drew wide circles with his arms and rotated his hips as though using an invisible hoop. These simple movements encourage the joints to move through their full range before the real work starts. He looked a little ridiculous, he knew, but nobody in the beginners' corner was laughing.

The best preparation for a lift, Ana explained, is a lighter version of the lift itself, because it lets the body rehearse the movement before any serious weight arrives. Kofi picked up the empty bar and performed a set of squats, thinking about his feet, his knees and his chest, and discovered that the movement now felt smoother than it had in the cold. The empty bar was, in effect, a polite introduction between his muscles and the work that lay ahead.

A lifter, Ana went on, does not leap straight from nothing to the heavy weight, but climbs towards it in what coaches call ramp-up sets. One set might use the empty bar, another a lighter load and a third something close to the weight of the day, each slightly more demanding than the last. It was like walking into a cold sea, she said, one step at a time instead of with a splash.

When Kofi finished his last set he was tempted to collapse onto the nearest bench, but Ana steered him instead into a slow walk around the gym with a towel across his shoulders. This short cool-down lets the heart rate and breathing settle gradually, and it feels pleasant, although the research on its benefits is not dramatic. For Kofi it became a small ritual of finishing, a way of closing the door gently behind him.

Sitting on a mat, Kofi extended one leg and reached slowly towards his foot, feeling a pleasant pull along the back of his thigh. Ana told him that stretching is enjoyable and may help flexibility over time, but that studies on whether it prevents soreness or injury have given mixed results. If he liked it, she said, he should do it; if he did not, nothing terrible would happen.

Tomas lent Kofi a foam roller, and Kofi rolled it slowly beneath his thigh with the grimace of a man who is being punished for a crime. Ana shrugged and said that many people love foam rolling and find that it helps them to feel looser, although scientific evidence for its benefits is still fairly modest. As with stretching, she told him, it is a pleasant extra rather than a requirement.

By the end of the month Kofi had designed a routine that he pinned to his fridge on a small card, with three lines written in blue pen: warm-up, workout and cool-down. All together it took about an hour, with ten minutes of warming up, forty of lifting and five of gently walking it off, and he found that it slipped easily into three evenings a week. A plan on the fridge, he discovered, is harder to ignore than a plan in the head.

On the blackboard Ana drew a row of small tally marks and introduced two words that Kofi would hear every day for the rest of his lifting life. One lift, she explained, is called a repetition, or a rep for short, and a group of reps done one after another without a proper break is called a set. It was a simple vocabulary, and Kofi understood it at once, and he repeated it to himself on the walk home.

Kofi asked how many reps make a good set, and Ana pointed to a chart on the wall. She told him that beginners commonly use somewhere between about five and ten, although lighter weights with more reps and heavier weights with fewer both build strength in their own ways. Nobody, she added, has proved that one single number is magical for everyone, so he could experiment as he learned.

For each of the five movements, Ana said, a beginner can do two or three sets, which adds up to a surprisingly small amount of work in a single session. Kofi wrote the numbers on his notepad and underlined them twice, relieved that the plan did not require him to live at the gym. A modest plan that is actually followed, she said, beats an ambitious one that is abandoned.

Between sets Kofi sat on a bench with his water bottle, watching the big clock on the wall and feeling his heartbeat slow down. Ana explained that rest matters, because muscles need a short recovery to produce good work again, and that heavier sets usually call for about one to three minutes. Checking his phone, she warned him with a smile, did not count as resting, because it never really lets the mind rest.

To help him choose the right weight, Ana taught Kofi a simple guideline that coaches often use. If he stopped each set while he could still have done two more good reps, he would have a couple of reps left in reserve, which keeps the work challenging but safe. It was a strange idea to a man who thought effort meant exhaustion, and it was a relief.

When the weight is right, Ana said, the last few reps feel hard, but the movement is still clean and the back stays flat and strong. If the form starts to fall apart, then the set is over, even if the number on the card says there are more to do. Kofi, who had always thought of stopping as failure, discovered that it could also be a skill.

Ana asked him to lift each dumbbell smoothly and to take about two seconds to lower it, instead of letting gravity do the work. A bouncing or swinging weight, she explained, takes the effort away from the muscles and puts it onto the joints, which is the opposite of what he wanted. Kofi tried it, and to his surprise the very same weight suddenly felt much heavier than before.

For the third time that evening, Kofi noticed that he was holding his breath, and Ana tapped her own chest as a reminder. Steady breathing makes a set easier, she said, and most people find it natural to breathe out while pushing or standing and to breathe in on the way back down. It sounded trivial, but it turned out to be one of the things that most improved his lifting in those early weeks.

Ana suggested that Kofi count his reps aloud, or at least silently in his head, instead of simply guessing when to stop. Counting gives the set a steady rhythm, she said, and it protects against the common beginner's habit of speeding up as the muscles begin to tire. By the end of the evening, half of the gym could hear him counting in a cheerful murmur.

At last Ana took a fresh card and wrote five exercises in a neat column, one from each of the five basic movements, with a small box for the weight beside each of them. Kofi would do two or three sets of each, with a warm-up before and a cool-down after, and for the first time in his life he was holding a real workout in his hand. It looked less like homework than like an invitation, and he folded it carefully and put it into his bag.

On a Monday evening, with his workout card in his pocket and a brand new notebook in his bag, Kofi walked into the gym feeling as nervous as he had on his first day at school. Ana greeted him at the door with a smile and a small nod that said she had every confidence in him. He found it hard to share her confidence, but he thanked her for it anyway.

The bar was light, and yet Kofi's arms trembled as he lifted it, and the very first set felt a great deal harder than anything he had imagined. He finished every set on the card, one slow repetition at a time, and with every one the trembling became a little less alarming. When the last set was done, he felt a quiet, unfamiliar sense of success.

Kofi walked out of the gym into the cool evening air, tired in a pleasant, heavy sort of way that he had not felt since childhood. On the bus home he leaned against the window and wondered how his body would feel in the morning, and a small part of him was already worried. He fell asleep that night faster than he had in years, and he slept without dreaming until the alarm rang.

The next morning Kofi discovered that his legs had gone on strike, and every stair at the office turned into a negotiation. He held the rail with both hands like a sailor crossing a deck in a storm, and a colleague in the lift asked him with genuine concern whether he had hurt himself. It was, he explained, a sign that he had been lifting weights, and he said it with unexpected pride.

Ana had warned him about this, and she now explained it properly: soreness a day or two after unfamiliar exercise is common, and it usually peaks around the second day. It eases within a few days, and the causes are not fully understood, although it is not usually a sign of anything serious when it is the ordinary kind. Knowing that, Kofi felt much calmer about every creak and twinge of his legs on the stairs that day.

Ana pointed to a knee on the wall chart and shook her head gently, because she wanted him to understand the difference between two kinds of discomfort. Soreness is a dull ache spread over the muscles, she said, but a sharp pain, a pain in a joint or a pain that does not go away is something else entirely. In that case he should stop, rest and ask a doctor or a physiotherapist for advice.

On his rest day Kofi went for a slow walk in the park, swinging his arms and feeling his legs gradually loosen with each step. Ana had told him that gentle movement on a day off, such as walking, often helps sore muscles to feel better, and that lying on the sofa for hours generally does not. It was a beautiful afternoon, and he stopped on a bridge to listen to the birds for a little while.

At his second workout Kofi was astonished to discover that the very same weights felt easier, and the soreness the following day was only a mild grumble. The body adapts remarkably quickly to a new kind of work, Ana told him, and the second time around it often protests much less. He felt as though his body and his mind had at last been properly introduced, and that they were getting along.

On a sheet of paper Ana drew a plan for the week: three gym days, with a day of rest tucked in between each pair. For a beginner, she said, two or three sessions a week is plenty, and the rest days are not wasted time but part of the training, because that is when the body recovers. Two sessions a week, she added, would still be a perfectly good start if three felt like too much.

Kofi stuck the plan on his fridge with a magnet shaped like a pineapple, and Adwoa, who was visiting that weekend, asked him what it was for. He told her proudly that he was getting stronger, and she looked him up and down with the doubtful expression of a very small inspector. Then she asked to see his muscles, and he flexed them with great ceremony while she pretended to be impressed.

On the whiteboard Ana drew a staircase with a small figure standing on the bottom step, and she explained the one idea that makes strength training work. The body adapts when it is asked for slightly more than it is used to, she said, and the name for this principle is progressive overload. Without it, a muscle has no real reason to change, and a body that is never challenged simply stays where it is.

Beneath the staircase Ana wrote a list: more weight, more reps, more sets, a slower lowering, a smoother and cleaner movement. Adding weight is only one of the ways to progress, she said, and on some days it is not the wisest. Kofi realised that he had many more tools than he had thought, and that none of them required him to be especially brave or to risk anything at all.

Kofi learned that weight should be added in small steps, and Ana showed him the smallest plates in the gym, thin and light and nearly comical beside their big brothers. He slid one onto each end of the bar and felt the difference in his hands straight away, which was just enough to be interesting without being alarming. It was progress, in miniature, and he could not have been more pleased if it had been the largest plate in the building.

Ana gave him a simple rule that he could keep in his head for every exercise. If he could complete all of his sets at the top of the rep range with clean form, he would add a little weight and begin again at the bottom of the range. The process would repeat whenever it was earned, and although it was neither dramatic nor fast, it worked.

Between sets, Kofi wrote the name of the exercise, the weight and the number of reps in his notebook, in handwriting that grew steadily less neat as he tired. Ana told him that a simple log shows progress and removes guesswork, and that memory is a poor accountant when it comes to personal achievements. Soon the notebook had become the most precious object in his gym bag, far more valuable than the bag itself.

After a month Kofi sat on a bench and flipped back through the pages of his notebook, watching the numbers climb quietly from one week to the next. On a rainy evening when he would rather have stayed at home, that small column of figures was a better argument than any speech or lecture. He put on his shoes, picked up his bag and went out into the rain.

Kofi was amazed at how quickly he was improving, and Ana, who had seen it many times, explained why. Early gains in strength come partly from the nervous system learning the movement, from better coordination and better use of the muscles already there, and only later from new muscle. It was, she said, like learning to ride a bicycle, in which the legs get no stronger but the rider gets better.

One evening Kofi, flushed with confidence, loaded the bar with far more weight than he usually used and tried to squat it. It barely moved, and he put it back with a sheepish grin while Ana raised an eyebrow without saying a word. Big jumps are tempting, she told him afterwards, but small steps almost always get you further and keep you safer.

After several months of training, Kofi stood in front of the gym mirror, rolled up his sleeves and studied his arms with the seriousness of an art critic. Something had changed, though it was subtle, and he could not have said exactly what it was. Ana reminded him that visible changes in muscle usually take weeks to months of regular training, and that strength arrives long before any show.

Two months in, Kofi placed his very first notebook next to his latest one and compared the two. The numbers on the first pages looked tiny, almost shy, beside the confident figures that filled the new one, and he could not stop grinning. Nobody else would ever understand how much those numbers meant to him, but Ana nodded when he showed her.

At his desk on Tuesday, Kofi unwrapped his usual lunch, which was a white sandwich and a bag of crisps, and ate it without noticing a single bite. Ana had told him that food is the fuel for training, and he began to wonder, rather uncomfortably, whether he had been driving a car on fumes for twenty years. He decided, there and then, to find out what a better lunch might look like, starting the very next day.

Protein, Ana explained, supplies the building blocks that muscles use to repair themselves and grow after training, and it is not hard to find. Eggs, beans, lentils, fish, chicken, yogurt, tofu and nuts all contain it, so most people can meet their needs from ordinary food without any special products. Kofi was relieved that the answer was not a shopping trip to a laboratory.

When Kofi asked exactly how much protein he needed, Ana did not give him a magic number, because she explained that needs differ from person to person. Official minimum recommendations are fairly modest, she said, and people who train often eat somewhat more, but a registered dietitian can offer advice that is suited to a person's age, health and goals. It was a question for a specialist, she said honestly, and not one that a gym coach should answer alone.

For years Kofi had imagined that a protein shake must be swallowed within minutes of leaving the gym, or the whole workout would be wasted. Ana told him that this idea is exaggerated, and that eating enough protein across the whole day appears to matter far more than the exact timing. He felt a weight lift from his mind, and a tub of powder lift from his shopping list.

Eating enough food overall, Ana went on, supports training, because muscles need energy as well as protein to do their work and to recover. Extreme dieting makes it harder to lift, harder to recover and often harder to keep going at all, so she advised him to avoid it. Kofi ate rice, vegetables and fish that evening and discovered that dinner could be a pleasure and a plan.

Before every session Kofi now filled his water bottle at the tap and sipped from it between sets, a habit that cost nothing and made the whole hour feel better. Ana told him that drinking water before, during and after exercise helps people to feel and perform well, and that pale yellow urine is a rough sign of being well hydrated. Thirst, she added, is also a perfectly good guide for most healthy people on most ordinary days of training.

Walking home, Kofi passed a shop window filled with large tubs of powders, each one promising enormous muscles within weeks. Ana had told him that most people do not need supplements, that food should come first, and that the claims on the labels are often exaggerated or only weakly supported. If he ever considered one, she said, he should ask a doctor or dietitian first.

On Sunday afternoon Kofi cooked a vast pot of bean stew with onions and tomatoes, stirring it with a wooden spoon and smelling the steam with great satisfaction. It was cheap and filling and full of protein, and the leftovers would give him lunch for the best part of the week. Strength, he decided, did not have to be expensive, complicated or sold to him in a tub with a picture of a bodybuilder.

At the market, Kofi filled his basket with different vegetables, fruits and grains, choosing whatever looked fresh and colourful rather than following any strict rule. Ana had told him that variety supports health in many ways, and that no single food, however famous, is magic or worth building a life around. He was glad that the advice was so ordinary, because it meant that he could actually follow it.

On a sunny Saturday Kofi and Adwoa walked to the park and shared an ice cream on a bench, and she told him very seriously that it was better than any gym snack. Ana had never once told him that a food was forbidden, because a balanced life, she said, is far easier to keep up than a strict one. He agreed with Adwoa, as a matter of principle, and ordered a second scoop for each of them.

After a week of late nights and early starts, Kofi yawned his way into the gym and nearly walked into the door. Ana looked at him sympathetically and told him something he had not expected to hear in a gym: muscles do not become stronger during the lifting itself, but during the rest and recovery that follow. A tired body, she said kindly, is not a lazy one, and it deserves some care and a good night in bed.

Most adults need about seven to nine hours of sleep a night, Ana said, although individuals vary and some people need a little more or less. Kofi, who had been managing five hours on a good night, was startled by how much of his flatness might be explained by this single number. Good sleep supports training, she added, and training in turn often helps people to sleep more deeply, although the effect differs from one person to another.

Kofi resolved to build himself a small evening routine, and he began by placing his phone on a shelf in the hallway instead of beside his bed. He turned down the lights an hour earlier, drank a glass of water and went to bed at roughly the same time each night. It felt childish at first, but within a week he was falling asleep faster and waking up with less of a groan.

On his rest days Kofi curled up in his armchair with a book and a pot of tea, quietly enjoying the strange luxury of doing nothing on purpose. Ana had explained that rest days are not a failure of discipline but an essential part of the plan, and that gentle movement, such as a walk, is always welcome. His legs, he noticed with some surprise, were grateful for both the book and the tea, and so was the rest of him.

Midway through a stressful week at work, with a pile of papers that grew taller every time he looked at it, Kofi felt tired in a way that had nothing to do with lifting. Ana told him that stress also takes energy from the body, and that when life is heavy it is perfectly reasonable to let the training be lighter. The gym, she said, should never become one more thing to dread, and on bad weeks it can simply be a place to move gently.

On days when he felt very tired, Kofi tried a trick: he went to the gym anyway but lifted lighter weights and did fewer sets, and he often felt better afterwards. Ana said that this was frequently wiser than skipping the session altogether, although she admitted that some days really do call for rest and that it takes experience to tell the difference. The skill of telling tiredness from laziness, she said, comes slowly, and Kofi would learn it only by trying and noticing.

When Kofi caught a heavy cold with a fever, he stayed at home under a blanket, drank tea with honey and did not lift so much as a teaspoon. Ana had told him that when you are properly ill, the sensible thing is to rest until you feel better, and that a doctor should be asked if the symptoms worry you. Returning with lighter weights afterwards, she added, is nothing to be embarrassed about, and it is usually the sensible way back to normal.

Feeling keen, Kofi decided to add a fourth gym day to his week, and for a while he felt like a champion in training. After ten days he felt flat and heavy-legged, his numbers stopped rising, and he began to dread the sessions instead of looking forward to them. Ana smiled kindly and reminded him that more is not always better, and that recovery is part of the work.

Scrolling through his phone, Kofi saw advertisements for massage guns, cold plunges and elaborate recovery gadgets, and wondered whether he needed any of them. Ana told him that the evidence for most of these is modest, that some people enjoy them and that nothing is wrong with enjoyment, but that sleep, food and plain rest come first. He felt quietly relieved to hear it, because it meant that his bank account could stay exactly as it was.

Sunday morning had become Kofi's favourite part of the week: he made a pot of tea, took a gentle walk by the river and looked ahead at the days to come. It had grown into a small ritual that gave his rest a purpose, and it helped him to plan his sessions around the rest of his busy life. For the first time in years, he looked after his body as carefully as he looked after his work, and he felt better for it.

One evening Kofi opened his notebook and saw that the numbers on the page had not changed for three weeks, and a cold feeling of disappointment crept into his stomach. He tried harder, grunted a little and wondered whether he had reached the end of what his body could do. The notebook, as it happens, did not care in the least how hard he had tried or how much he wanted a change.

On the whiteboard Ana sketched a curve that rose steeply, flattened out and rose again more slowly, and she explained that this is how nearly everyone's progress looks. Gains come fast at the beginning, when there is a great deal to learn, and slower later, so a plateau is a normal part of training and not a sign of failure. Kofi stared at the curve for a long moment and felt oddly comforted, as if someone had told him that the road really was uphill.

Before changing anything, Ana asked Kofi to check the basics, and she ticked them off on a list as he answered. How much was he sleeping, was he eating enough, was the week at work especially stressful and had he really attended every session? Kofi admitted that two of the four had been wobbling lately, and the problem suddenly looked smaller.

Ana took out her phone, filmed his squat from the side as she had done on the first day and played the video back to him. He saw at once that his form had slipped, because his chest was falling forward and his knees were drifting inward, as if the weights had slowly taught him bad habits. When he corrected both of them, the very same weight felt a little lighter, and his set looked much smoother.

The next plate on the rack looked like too big a jump, so Kofi decided to add just one extra repetition to each set instead. Ana approved, saying that adding a single rep, or using the smallest plates, keeps progress moving gently and avoids the shock of a big leap. It was a modest change, but it worked exactly as she had promised, and his notebook finally showed a small, pleasing number.

On the calendar Ana coloured one week in a pale shade and wrote the word easy across it in large letters. An easier week every now and then, she said, is called a deload, and it gives the body a chance to recover fully and absorb the work it has done. Some lifters plan one regularly, whether they feel tired or not, and taking one is not a sign of weakness.

In his deload week Kofi lifted light weights, did fewer sets and walked around the almost empty gym like a visitor in a museum. It felt strange to finish a session still feeling fresh, and he wondered whether anything useful could possibly be happening. Ana only said that he should trust the plan for one week, and that he could be as suspicious as he liked.

When the deload week was over, Kofi walked into the gym feeling fresh and a little restless, as a horse might feel after a rest in a field. The bar felt lighter than it had a month earlier, and for the first time in weeks the numbers in his notebook began to climb again. He wrote the new numbers down with a flourish, underlined them twice and closed the notebook with a grin.

Climbing the stairs to his flat one evening, Kofi suddenly realised that he was hardly breathing hard, and that he had been carrying two bags without noticing. Ana had told him that strength shows itself in many ways, such as stairs, sleep, mood and energy, and not only in the numbers in the notebook. Life, it seemed, was keeping its own and more generous log, one that never needed a pencil to record the progress.

One evening Kofi watched a very strong man lift an enormous bar across the gym, and he felt a familiar pang of envy and doubt. Ana noticed his expression and told him that comparing yourself with other people is rarely helpful, because everyone starts from a different place and with a different life. The only fair comparison, she said, is with yourself a month ago, and there Kofi was winning.

On a busy Wednesday evening, Kofi stood at the edge of the free-weight area with a dumbbell in his hand, convinced that every person in the room was waiting to judge him. His heart was pounding, his palms were damp and he very nearly turned around and went home. It was the old feeling, the one that had kept him outside the glass door for a week.

Then he looked around properly and saw something that surprised him: nobody was looking at him at all. A man was frowning at a mirror, a woman was counting under her breath, two friends were arguing over a playlist and everyone else was lost in their own workout and their own thoughts. The audience that he had feared so much simply was not there, and he felt both foolish and wonderfully free.

Ana had taught him that good manners in a gym begin with a towel, and so after each use Kofi wiped down the bench and the handles before leaving them. It was a small courtesy, but it made the place cleaner and made him feel like a proper member rather than a trespasser. The next person, he thought, would never know, and that was exactly the point.

When he finished a lift, Kofi took the plates off the bar and put them back on the rack, and he slid the bar into its place on the wall. Leaving weights lying about is more than discourteous, Ana explained, because someone can trip over them or struggle to move them when they are in a hurry. Tidying up was a way of saying thank you to everyone else in the room.

Kofi wanted to use the cable machine, but a man was resting beside it with a towel around his neck, and for a moment Kofi hovered nervously. Then he remembered Ana's advice and asked politely whether the man was still using it, and the man smiled and said that they could easily share it. Gyms, it turned out, are run mostly on small kindnesses of this kind, and he was glad to have found one.

Between sets, Kofi moved away from the bench and rested on a stool a few steps away, so that other people could use the equipment in the meantime. He kept his phone in his bag, because scrolling for ten minutes on a bench that someone else is waiting for is, Ana said, the one thing that really annoys people. It was one of the very few unwritten rules that really mattered, and it cost him nothing at all to follow.

Kofi could not work out how to adjust the seat of the chest machine, and for several minutes he pretended that he knew exactly what he was doing. At last he walked to the front desk and asked Tomas, who came over at once and set the pin in the right place with a cheerful click. Asking for help, Kofi realised, was a sign of good sense and not of weakness.

After the evening session, Mrs Okafor paused by the beginners' corner to say hello to Kofi, her eyes bright and her handshake surprisingly firm. She invited him to come and watch her Tuesday class, and she told him that she had once been just as nervous as he was. Kofi said that he would be delighted to come along, and he meant every word of it.

Many people at Riverside wore headphones and listened to music while they lifted, and Kofi tried it himself and found that a good song could carry him through a hard set. Others preferred silence, and Ana told him that respecting one another's space, in whichever way, is part of being a good neighbour in a gym. He turned the volume down a little after that, in case anyone nearby wanted to talk to him.

As Kofi left the gym that evening, he said goodnight to Tomas, waved to Mrs Okafor and held the door for a young woman carrying a heavy bag. He realised, with a small start of surprise, that he knew the names of several members now, and that the place no longer felt like somebody else's territory. It had quietly become his own, in the gentle way that a favourite chair or a favourite street slowly does.

Kofi sat down at the chest press machine and pushed the handles away from his body along a smooth, fixed path that left him no choice about where to go. Ana explained that machines guide the movement, which makes them a safe and sensible place for beginners to start, and that they also let people train close to their limit without needing a spotter. It felt reassuring to Kofi, rather like cycling with stabilisers on a bicycle for the very first time.

Before he began, Ana showed him how to adjust the seat height, the handle position and the weight pin, which she called the three settings that everyone forgets. A machine can only do its work well when it fits your body, she said, and a poorly adjusted one can leave you feeling awkward or even uncomfortable. It took a full minute to set everything up properly, and it was a minute that he was glad to have spent.

Free weights, by contrast, do not follow any fixed path, and the body has to balance and steer the load for itself. This trains many more muscles at the same time, Ana explained, including the small stabilising ones that machines tend to leave alone, but it also demands more skill and a little more care. Kofi found that a dumbbell seemed to have its own opinions about where it wished to go, while a machine merely had handles.

When Kofi asked which of the two was better, Ana raised both hands like the pans of a pair of scales and let them wobble. Neither is best for everyone, she said, and research on beginners suggests that both can build strength well, with free weights perhaps carrying over a little better to everyday balance. She advised him to enjoy both kinds, to stop worrying about which one was the winner and to get on with his lifting.

Standing by the rack, Ana pointed out that dumbbells train each side of the body separately, which can show up a weaker arm or leg and help it to catch up. A barbell, on the other hand, makes it easy to add very small amounts of weight and to lift heavier loads over time, so both have a proper place in a sensible plan. Kofi felt that the whole argument had been settled very politely, with no winners and a good deal of sense.

In the beginners' corner Ana lifted a kettlebell by its handle and held it close to her chest like a baby bird, explaining that it is excellent for goblet squats and carries. The handle is easy to hold and the weight sits neatly in front of the body, she said, although swings are a more advanced skill. They are best learned with a coach standing nearby, she added, so Kofi gladly left the swinging for later, when he had a few more months behind him.

Ana handed Kofi a long rubber band and asked him to hold one end under his foot and pull the other towards his chest. Bands are light, cheap and easy to carry in a bag, and the further they stretch, the harder they pull, which means that the exercise gets heavier as it goes. He bought two bands for himself on the way out of the gym, in two different colours, and tucked them into his bag.

At the tall cable machine Kofi pulled a handle smoothly across his chest, feeling a steady tension that did not change as it moved. Ana explained that cables give a smooth and even resistance, and that with different handles and heights they can be used for rows, pulldowns and a great many other exercises. It was like having a whole small gym folded neatly into a single, tall and well-organised tower of weights.

Ana reminded Kofi that his own body weight is a complete, free and very flexible way to train, with no equipment needed at all. Squats, press-ups and step-ups can be made easier by changing the angle or the depth and harder by slowing down or adding a pause, so a beginner and an expert can use the same exercise. This was comforting, because it meant that he could always train, wherever he happened to be and whatever the weather was doing.

On Friday Kofi sat with his notebook and planned the session, mixing two machines with three free-weight movements and a short carry at the end. Ana looked at the page and smiled, because the best exercise, she told him, is the one that you will actually do, and Kofi had finally found a mix that he enjoyed. It was a small plan, but it was entirely his own, and it was the first one that he had made without Ana's help.

A notice on the gym door announced that Riverside would be closed for a week of repairs, and Kofi read it three times as if it might change. He stood in the drizzle with his sports bag and felt the old reluctance stir, the voice that said a week off might easily become a month. Then he thought of his notebook and the numbers in it, turned around and walked briskly home through the rain.

At home he pushed the sofa against the wall, rolled out a mat and put on his trainers, and a living room that had always been for resting became a small, humble gym. All that a home workout really needs, Ana had told him, is a small clear space, a firm floor and sensible shoes, and everything else is a bonus. He looked around the cramped little room, with its lamp and its curtains, and decided that he had plenty.

Kofi sat down on a sturdy kitchen chair and stood up again, slowly and carefully, with his arms held out in front of him for balance. A chair works in just the same way as the wooden box at the gym, because it tells the body where to stop and where to start, and it makes a very good first squat. He did three whole sets of squats while the kettle boiled, and he was finished before the tea was ready.

Kofi loaded a backpack with a stack of heavy books, held it against his chest and squatted down to the chair with the satisfied air of a man who has beaten the system. He could add one book at a time, which was a perfect way to follow Ana's rule of small steps without spending a penny. The only real difficulty was deciding which of his old novels to sacrifice to the cause that afternoon.

Kofi put his hands on the edge of the kitchen counter and lowered his chest towards it, his body in a straight line from head to heels. Press-ups can be done against a wall, a counter or the floor, Ana had said, depending on how strong a person feels that day, and the choice of surface lets anyone adjust the difficulty. Today the counter was exactly the right height for him, and he finished every repetition without a single wobble.

Kofi looped a rubber band around a door anchor, a small strap made for the purpose, and stepped back until the band was tight, then pulled it towards his stomach like a rower. Ana had warned him to check the band for cracks and the door for firmness before every session, because a band that snaps can sting badly. He tested both of them twice, and to his relief they were perfectly fine, so he began his first set of rows.

In the kitchen, Kofi filled two large milk jugs with water, screwed on the caps and carried them around like a pair of oddly shaped dumbbells. A litre of water weighs about one kilogram, so he could calculate the weights without any difficulty, and he could pour out a little or add a little as he saw fit. It was the cheapest and most adjustable equipment that he had ever owned, and the tap in his kitchen supplied it for free.

At the park, Kofi stepped up onto a low bench again and again, switching legs, and then walked a full lap of the path with two heavy shopping bags to practise his carries. Nobody gave him a second look, and he realised that the world was far too busy to notice a man exercising in a coat. He walked home with a pleasant ache in his legs and a pleasantly empty head, feeling lighter than he had all week.

By the end of the week at home, Kofi had understood something about the two kinds of training, and he explained it to himself on the bus. Training at home saves time and travel and has no waiting, he thought, while a gym offers heavier weights, expert eyes and the company of other people, and there was no reason to choose only one. Most people, Ana later told him, end up mixing both in some way that suits their own lives, budgets and timetables.

On Saturday morning Adwoa arrived with a bag of crayons and an urgent need to be included, so Kofi announced that she was in charge of the workout. She crawled like a bear across the living room floor, hopped like a frog and waddled like a duck, and Kofi laughed so hard that he had to follow her. It was, he realised later that evening on the sofa, easily the most strenuous and the most enjoyable hour of his whole week.

On the wall of the beginners' corner Ana taped a short checklist in her large, round handwriting, and she asked every newcomer to read it. The floor should be clear, the equipment checked, the warm-up done and the weight sensible, it said, and nothing on the list was complicated or hard to remember. Kofi decided that it was exactly the kind of list that he would have liked to read years ago.

Before a heavy press on the bench, Ana stood behind Kofi as a spotter, hands hovering near the bar but never touching it unless it was needed. A spotter is a person who stands ready to help if a lift goes wrong, she explained, and it is polite as well as wise to agree on signals beforehand. Kofi's job was to ask clearly and in good time, and Ana's job was to be ready, calm and close by.

The squat rack had a pair of metal safety bars that could catch the weight if a lift went wrong, and Ana showed Kofi how to set them at the right height, just below the lowest point of his squat. They are there for emergencies, she said, and she hoped he would never need them, but a safety net that is set badly is no net at all. He checked them twice every time he went near the rack, and he never once felt that it was a waste of time.

One evening a man in the free-weight area loaded far too much weight on to the bar, lifted it with a roar and dropped it with a crash that made the whole room look up. Lifting more than you can control, just to impress somebody, Ana said afterwards, is the most common way for anyone to get hurt in a gym. Kofi made a quiet note to leave his ego in the changing room from then on, along with his coat and his keys.

Kofi had always feared that lifting weights would harm his back, and he finally asked Ana about it, almost whispering. She explained that, for most people, gradual strength training is thought to be good for the back, because it strengthens the muscles that support the spine, although anyone with existing back pain should see a doctor or physiotherapist before beginning. It was a more balanced answer than the myths he had heard, and he trusted it more.

Ana was clear about warning signs, and she wanted Kofi to remember them for as long as he trained. Chest pain, dizziness, severe shortness of breath or a sudden sharp pain all mean that you should stop lifting at once and get medical help, and no workout is ever worth ignoring them. Kofi wrote them on the inside cover of his notebook, in capital letters, and hoped never to need them.

Dr Mensah had examined Kofi carefully, listened to his chest, taken his blood pressure and asked a long list of questions before declaring that a gentle start was perfectly fine. She added a few suggestions that were specific to him, which Ana could never have given, and Kofi was grateful that he had gone to see her first. A coach, Ana agreed, is a friend to your training and not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health.

Before the next session Kofi sat on the edge of his bed and tied a pair of flat, firm shoes, checking that his laces were secure and double-knotted. Ana had told him that flat shoes with a firm sole help the feet to feel the floor, and that comfortable clothes, which do not restrict movement, make lifting both safer and more pleasant. Soft running shoes with thick heels, she said with a smile, are better left for running than for heavy lifting.

One evening Kofi felt a twinge in his shoulder during a press, and he put the dumbbells down and rubbed it with a frown. Ana swapped the exercise for another one at once and told him that a sharp or persistent pain should never be ignored, and that if it lasted he ought to see a professional. They worked on his legs for the rest of the night, and the shoulder recovered within a few days.

Ana reminded him that, when it is done sensibly, strength training has a fairly low risk of injury, particularly when compared with many popular sports. Being weak also has its own risks, such as falls and strains in everyday life, so she thought that the balance was clearly in favour of sensible lifting. Kofi felt better about the whole adventure, and he stood a little taller on the way out.

On Tuesday Kofi sat at the back of Mrs Okafor's class with his notebook on his knee, watching a dozen older members lift light dumbbells with an air of calm concentration. They moved together like a slow, friendly orchestra, laughing at their own mistakes and praising each other's successes. He had expected a gentle waiting room, and what he found was a team.

Halfway through the class, Mrs Okafor stood up from a low chair without using her hands, as easily as if she were rising to greet a guest, and Kofi's mouth fell open. Ana whispered that strength training helps older adults with balance, with preventing falls and with staying independent, which is why health organisations widely recommend it. Kofi thought of his own mother, who was seventy and lived on the other side of the city, and made a private promise.

In the free-weight area, several women were lifting barbells and dumbbells with enthusiasm, and Kofi could see that none of them was becoming bulky or bearing any resemblance to the cartoon images he remembered from magazines. Women build strength in the same way as men, Ana told him, although often with less muscle size, and nobody gets large by accident. The idea that weights will make women bulky, she said firmly, is a myth that has been repeated for far too long.

One evening a teenager came in with his father and lifted a very light bar while a coach watched every move with the intensity of a hawk. Teenagers can train with weights too, Ana explained, provided that the loads are light, the coaching is good and technique comes first, and a doctor should be asked if there is any doubt. For young people, as for everyone else in the gym, the secret is patience and a good teacher at the start.

Kofi noticed a man who was rowing with a rubber band from his wheelchair, back straight and shoulders working, and he asked Ana about him afterwards in a low voice. She told him that exercises can be adapted to suit a very wide range of bodies, and that a qualified coach or physiotherapist can design a safe version for almost anyone. There is no single right body for lifting, she said, only the one that you have.

Mrs Okafor taught her class a simple exercise called the sit-to-stand, which involves sitting on a chair, folding the arms across the chest and rising without any help from the hands. It sounds almost insultingly easy, she told them with a twinkle, until the day it is hard, and then it becomes the most important exercise in the world. Kofi did ten of them in a row and found that his thighs strongly disagreed with the word easy, which made Mrs Okafor laugh.

At home that night Kofi stood in front of the bathroom mirror, lifted one foot from the floor and brushed his teeth while balancing on the other leg. Balance can be trained like any other skill, Ana had told him, and it matters more and more as people grow older, because a good sense of balance helps to prevent falls. He wobbled badly for the first ten seconds and nearly dropped his toothbrush, and then, slowly and to his surprise, he improved.

On the whiteboard Ana drew a bone with small arrows pressing down on it, and she explained that bones respond to load much as muscles do. Weight-bearing and resistance exercise are linked with stronger bones, she said, which matters particularly for older people and for women after the menopause, although it works best alongside good nutrition and the advice of a doctor. Kofi, who was only forty-four and had no worries about the menopause, copied the drawing carefully into his notebook anyway.

Mrs Okafor showed Kofi an old, slightly faded photograph from a research article, in which a group of elderly people sat in a care home lifting small weights and smiling for the camera. Studies of this kind have found strength gains even in people in their eighties and nineties, she said, and she took that as proof that it is never too late to begin. Kofi felt a lump rise in his throat and laughed loudly to hide it, and Mrs Okafor, who understood, patted his arm.

That evening Kofi telephoned his mother, Efua, who was seventy, and explained the sit-to-stand to her in the most careful voice he could manage. She laughed at first and said that she had been standing up from chairs for seventy years, but then she propped her phone on the table and tried it, and before long she was counting aloud. By the end of the call she had asked him to teach her a second exercise.

Walking to the gym one bright afternoon, Kofi noticed that he was in a good mood for no particular reason and that he was swinging his arms as he went. Ana told him that exercise is linked, on average, with better mood and less anxiety, although it affects people differently and is never a replacement for proper care when someone is struggling. He took it as a pleasant bonus of the training and not as a promise, and he enjoyed the walk all the more.

After a workout Kofi stood tall in front of the glass door, his shoulders back and a calm, private smile on his face, and he realised that he was not afraid of walking into rooms any more. He felt more confident at work and at home, a change that nobody had warned him about, although Ana reminded him that results vary a good deal from one person to another. He accepted this unexpected gift without arguing, and he carried it with him all the way home that evening.

One wet and windy evening Kofi stood at his front door with his bag in his hand, listening to the rain drumming on the roof and thinking how lovely it would be to stay in. Ana had told him that consistency matters far more than perfection, and that the rainy evening is the real test of any plan, so he sighed, put on his shoes and went. He was very glad afterwards that he had gone, and he told himself that the rain had been the best part of it.

After a week away in bed with a cold, Kofi worried that he had lost everything he had gained and that he would have to start again from the first page of his notebook. He returned with lighter weights and no guilt, as Ana had suggested, and within two sessions he was back almost where he had been. A short pause, he discovered, erases far less of your progress than the anxious mind imagines in the dark.

Kofi kept his gym bag packed beside the front door, and he circled his gym days on the calendar in blue pen so that they looked like appointments with a very important person. Ana had told him that habits grow from a fixed time, an easy first step and a link to something that already happens every day. A bag by the door, he found, was half of the battle already won, because nobody likes to walk past it and do nothing.

In his notebook Kofi wrote two kinds of goals on a clean page, one marked with a circle for what he would do and one marked with a star for what he hoped would happen. Goals about actions, such as three sessions a week, are far easier to control than goals about results, Ana said, because you can always keep a promise to yourself even when the scale or the mirror refuses to cooperate. He underlined the circle twice, because those were the goals that he could keep, whatever the weather and whatever the mirror said.

A colleague called Daniel, who had noticed Kofi's new energy at the office and said so over the photocopier, asked if he might come along to the gym one evening. Training with a friend makes it easier to turn up on the days when you do not feel like it, Ana said, because it is harder to let down another person than yourself. Kofi was glad of the company, and slightly proud to be asked, since nobody had ever asked him for fitness advice before.

Between sets, Kofi and Daniel listened with pained expressions to the gym's playlist, which seemed to consist entirely of strange old songs, and they laughed until Ana told them to behave. Enjoyment is the quiet secret of people who keep training for years, she said, so music, friends and a little variety are all perfectly legitimate parts of the plan. It was not supposed to feel like punishment, after all, and from that evening on he made sure that it never did.

Sitting in the park one Sunday, Kofi looked at a tall oak growing next to a small sapling and thought about how slowly both of them were changing, in a way that no one could see from day to day. Progress over years comes from patience, Ana had said, and a bad week or even a bad month is simply a part of any long journey. The little sapling, he decided, was a very good sign, and he promised himself to come back and look at it next year.

Six months after their first race, Adwoa challenged Kofi to another one on the stairs of his block of flats, and she set off with her usual confident shout. This time Kofi reached the top first, breathing steadily and grinning, while she arrived a few seconds later with her mouth wide open in astonishment. Before he could even catch his breath, she was already demanding a rematch, and he gladly agreed to run again.

One sunny Saturday in the park, Kofi showed Daniel how to squat down to a wooden box, using the very same words that Ana had used on his first day. Start light, learn the movement and add a little at a time, he told him, and he noticed that teaching it made it clearer in his own mind. Daniel wobbled, laughed and tried again, and Kofi felt a quiet glow of pride.

One evening Kofi and Ana stood beside the whiteboard and looked back at the five drawings that had started everything. They went through the squat, the hinge, the push, the pull and the carry in turn, and Kofi realised how much each of them had taught him about his legs, his back, his arms and his patience. The little ticks were faded now, but he could still remember the day and the evening on which he had earned every one.

At the gym cafe Kofi leafed through a thick book of training programmes, with names and numbers and cleverly drawn tables, and he began to feel both curious and slightly dizzy. There are many programmes, and each one has its devoted fans, but no single programme is the best for everyone, because people differ in their goals, their bodies and their lives. He closed the book gently, ordered another cup of tea and decided that his current plan was good enough for now.

Ana told him that, once the basics were solid, there would be plenty of time to explore other methods if he was curious, and he should not feel any pressure to do so. A coach can give feedback that no book ever can, she added, because a coach can see the person and the movement, and Kofi should feel free to ask for that help whenever he wanted it. He nodded slowly, thinking of his very first lesson, when a stranger in a blue shirt had shaken his hand at the door.

Late one night, Kofi read two articles on his laptop that disagreed about almost everything, and each one seemed completely sure of itself. Ana told him the next day that research changes, that people differ, and that very confident claims are a good reason for caution, so he should prefer reliable sources and be ready to change his mind. It was, Kofi thought, the most useful thing that she had said all week, and he wrote it at the back of his notebook.

Kofi set himself a new goal, a long walk up the green hill behind the town with Adwoa, each of them carrying a small backpack with a sandwich and an apple. Strength supports the things that you love doing, Ana had said, and he realised that he wanted to be able to keep going up hills for as long as there were hills to climb. He circled the date in his calendar in blue pen, and he started to look forward to it as he had once looked forward to nothing.

A year after his first day at the gym, Kofi stood in his living room and looked at the three full notebooks that now sat on the shelf, their covers curled and their pages crowded with numbers. Ana, when he showed them to her, said that she was proud of him, and that she would see him on Monday as usual. Nothing, he thought as he walked home that evening, had ever sounded so reassuring, or so wonderfully ordinary.

Kofi opened a fresh notebook and wrote a few short rules inside the front cover, in capital letters that he had practised: start light, learn the movement, add a little, rest well and keep turning up. They were not clever rules, and he knew that experts might want to add to them or argue with them. They were, however, his own, and they had worked for him, which was the only test that really mattered.

On a wet evening, as Kofi arrived at Riverside Gym, he noticed a man standing outside the glass door with a brand new sports bag, looking through the glass as though it were a shop window. Kofi remembered that feeling so well that it almost hurt, and he stopped, smiled and said that the first step is the hardest one. Then he pushed the heavy glass door open with his shoulder and held it wide, so that the man could walk in.

Kofi and Ana stood side by side in the middle of the gym, each holding a light dumbbell, and the room hummed quietly around them. To begin lifting, you need only a light weight, a few basic movements, a little patience and the willingness to add a little at a time and to keep turning up. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor or a qualified coach about your own body and your own needs.
